1 · Quick start

  1. Click anywhere once so the browser allows alarm sound. Check the top bar shows 🔔 Sound on.
  2. The session opens at design: batch reactor R-101 (140 m³) is 2.0 h into the reaction — 60 t of water and 51 t of vinyl chloride (VCM) at 57.0 °C and 8.6 bar g, 26 % converted to PVC, releasing about 2.7 MW. The jacket, four water-cooled baffles and the reflux condenser E-101 take the heat away. Open Process to learn the chemistry, P&ID for the drawings, then DCS console to operate.
  3. A batch never stands still: conversion, heat release and pressure change all the time. The dashed curves on the Batch progress display show the reference batch; your batch should follow them.
  4. Go to Exercises, pick a list (Training, Think EQUIPPED or Procedures) and click Load. A blue banner gives the situation; click Acknowledge on the banner to hide it.
  5. Operate from the DCS console (click a bubble, motor or valve to open its faceplate on the right) and from Batch & SIS (charging, initiator, short-stop, degassing, discharge). Use Speed (up to 200×) for the long parts of a batch and Freeze to think.
  6. When finished, open Debrief and grading for your score, then Data export for CSV files.

2 · Top bar

ClockSimulated time since the session (exercise) started. The reaction time since the initiator is on the Overview display and the Batch & SIS tab.
Freeze / SpeedPause, or run 1–200× faster. The model runs in 0.25 s steps at every speed.
Status lampGreen while reacting normally, amber when not reacting (charging, heat-up, end of batch), red when the SIS has tripped. Click it to open Batch & SIS.
Sound, Silence, AcknowledgeAudible alarm on/off; Silence stops the horn until the next new alarm; Acknowledge acknowledges every alarm.
ScoreContinuous score (see Debrief).

The tabs are in six groups. Click a group in the top row; its tabs appear in the second row (on a phone, in a drop-down). A few pages sit in two groups because they belong to both: P&ID (Process & Design and Operate), Safety layers (Process & Design and Safety) and SOP (Operability and Train & Assess). The page opens on Operate.

4 · DCS console

Displays: Overview (batch status), Heat removal (where the 2–3.5 MW goes and how much margin is left), Batch progress (pressure and conversion against the reference batch, K-value, end point) and Economics. Each instrument bubble shows letters (e.g. TIC), loop number and its live value; controllers show their mode (MAN / AUTO / CAS). Lines are coloured by service: blue VCM / slurry, dark blue water, purple VCM gas and vents, teal cooling water, red steam, grey nitrogen. Dashed lines carry no flow. The liquid in R-101 whitens as PVC forms; a grey band at the top of E-101 shows inerts blanketing its tubes.

5 · Faceplates

Click a bubble: the faceplate shows PV, SP and output bars, mode buttons (Manual, Automatic, Cascade), set point and output fields with −/+ steps, a note on how the loop works in this unit, the tuning (gain, reset, rate) and the alarm limits. Cascades: TIC-100 → TIC-110 (reactor → jacket inlet, split range steam/CW), LIC-100 → FIC-103 (level → shrinkage water), VPC-130 → FIC-130 (jacket valve position → E-101 water). A slave must be in CAS for its master to act.

6 · Trends and alarms

Choose a trend group or Selected tag (PV, SP, OUT of the selected loop); windows 5–60 min. Alarms list newest unacknowledged first; click to acknowledge and select the tag. Process alarms are suppressed when they do not apply (for example the temperature band only while reacting).

7 · Batch & SIS

The batch sequence: Evacuate (XV-109) → Charge water (XV-101, FQ preset) → Charge VCM (XV-102, needs permissives) → heat-up on steam → Charge initiator (XV-103, at ≥ 54 °C) → reaction → end point → Short-stop (XV-104) → Degas (XV-105 + HIC-105) → N₂ pad (Field) → Discharge (XV-106). The SIS short-stops the batch on TSHH-101, PSHH-101, agitator stopped or jacket circulation lost while reacting; LSHH-100 stops the charges. Reset needs the cause cleared.

8 · Field

Start and stop M-101, P-101A/B and P-103; open HV-107 (PVA pot, during the water charge) and HV-141 (N₂ pad, for discharge). Outside checks describe what an operator would see and hear. The laboratory reports conversion, residual VCM, K-value and the coarse fraction after 2 minutes.

9 · Exercises

Training: one fault each from the design batch. Think EQUIPPED: a symptom with hidden causes — work through Engage, Define, Explore, Plan, Do it, Look back. Procedures are graded: cold start, end of batch, pump failure, runaway prevention, condenser upset and cooling-water optimisation. What-if compares your predictions with an undisturbed copy of the batch 30 minutes later.

10 · Debrief and data export

The score starts at 100; points come off while the temperature is outside 57 ± 0.5 °C during the reaction, the pressure is above 11 bar g, the level is out of band, the K-value drifts or lumps form, safety limits are crossed, foam fouls E-101, alarms sit unacknowledged or the SIS trips. Export run data, a snapshot against design, or the event log as CSV. Nothing is kept after the page closes.

11 · Symbols and colours

Valves: green open, red closed, grey modulating (% shown). On/off valves carry an S box. Motors: green running, red stopped. Bubbles with a square frame are SIS; bubbles are colour-coded by loop family (red temperature, teal cooling water, green level, blue feed, purple vents).

Process: suspension polymerisation of vinyl chloride in R-101

110 slides in eight parts, with sliders and virtual labs. Opens over this page; ← → to move, T for contents, Esc or × to close.

1 · Operating principles

Chemistry. n CH₂=CHCl → (–CH₂–CHCl–)ₙ, free-radical chain growth, −71 kJ/mol (1.14 MJ/kg PVC, the basis of the reference card's 200 kt/y → 7.9 MW). Organic peroxide initiators decompose into radicals; each radical adds thousands of VCM molecules in milliseconds.

Suspension. VCM (0.85 t/m³, boils at −13 °C) is dispersed as 30–150 µm droplets in water by the agitator and a suspending agent (PVA). Each droplet is a small bulk reactor; the water carries the heat to the walls. Without agitation the droplets rise, coalesce and form lumps.

PVC is insoluble in its monomer. It precipitates inside each droplet as a gel that holds about 28 % VCM. While free liquid VCM remains (conversion below Xf ≈ 0.72) the reactor pressure is simply the vapour pressure of VCM at the temperature (≈ 9.2 bar a at 57 °C) plus water and inerts — it does not change with conversion. Beyond Xf the monomer left is only in the gel, its activity falls and the pressure drops: a set pressure drop (1.8 bar here, ≈ 85 % conversion) is the end point.

Temperature sets the grade. Chain length (K-value) is fixed mainly by chain transfer to monomer, a function of temperature only: 57 °C gives K 67, each °C about −0.6 K. The whole batch must be held within about ± 0.5 °C.

Heat release and runaway. The gel effect speeds the reaction as conversion rises while the fast initiator is used up; a fast + slow initiator pair keeps the release fairly flat — 1.7 MW at the start, a peak of ≈ 3.4 MW near X ≈ 0.7. The release grows ≈ 9 % per °C, the removal only ≈ 4–5 % per °C: the reactor is open-loop unstable and relies on control and on cooling margin. A short-stop (radical scavenger) ends the reaction at the end point or in an emergency.

Why a reflux condenser. Volume grows with D³, jacket area with D². At 140 m³ the jacket (≈ 1.5–1.8 MW) plus baffles (0.4 MW) cannot carry the peak; E-101 adds area by letting VCM boil off the slurry, condensing it and returning it — as the reference card says, “the jacket runs out as the vessel grows, so a condenser adds the missing area”.

2 · Block flow diagram

3 · Process description

Preparation. After the previous batch R-101 is washed and closed. XV-109 evacuates it to below 0.05 bar a so that almost no air is left: oxygen delays the start of the reaction and nitrogen collects in E-101.

Charging. 60 t of demineralised water at 55 °C (FIC-101, FQI-101 preset) goes in with the PVA from TK-107 (HV-107). The agitator M-101 starts once the lower impeller is covered. P-103 then charges 51 t of VCM (FIC-102, FQI-102). The mixture settles near 46 °C and 6.5 bar g.

Heat-up and initiation. TIC-110 heats the jacket loop with LP steam injected through TV-110A into SM-101 (≈ 20 min). At 54–57 °C TIC-100 takes over in cascade and the initiator is charged from D-104 (XV-103): the reaction time starts. A few minutes of induction follow while the last oxygen is consumed.

Reaction. TIC-100 (57.0 °C) sets TIC-110; its output opens CW injection TV-110B (the same mass spills to CWR). The baffles run on 80 m³/h of CW. E-101 comes in as the conversion passes a few percent — its water is clamped to 12 m³/h per % of XI-100 so that the boil-up cannot lift foam into the tubes — and VPC-130 then moves load onto E-101 so that TV-110B stays near 50 % open. HIC-135 vents the inerts that collect at the top of E-101. LIC-100 keeps 83 % level with shrinkage water (FIC-103).

End of batch. At ≈ 5.3 h the free VCM is gone and PI-100 falls; when PD-100 reaches 1.8 bar the short-stop is injected (XV-104). The unreacted VCM (≈ 7.5 t) is degassed to recovery (XV-105, HIC-105) down to 2 bar g; an N₂ pad (HV-141) then pushes the slurry (≈ 130 t, 43 t PVC) through XV-106 to blowdown tank D-102 for stripping and drying.

Safety. TSHH-101 (63 °C), PSHH-101 (12.5 bar g), agitator stopped (XS-101) and jacket circulation lost (FSLL-110) short-stop the batch and put every cooler on full; LSHH-100 stops the charges; PSV-100 (15 bar g) relieves to the dump tank; the ESD also opens XV-108.

Teaching slide deck — polymerisation kinetics and heat release, pressure of a VCM batch, jacket / baffle / reflux-condenser heat removal, runaway, operating conditions and conceptual sizing of R-101.
Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

How a suspension-PVC reactor like R-101 (one of four identical 140 m³ reactors, 200 kt/y in total) is specified and roughed out before detailed design. Every number on this page comes from the R-101 model: the reference batch (start of reaction at 57 °C, 60 t water + 51 t VCM, noise off) and the design state 2.0 h into the reaction. Section 5 is a conceptual sizing, not a vendor rating.

1 Fundamentals and principle · 2 Components · 3 Setting the operating conditions · 4 Conceptual design · 5 Conceptual sizing (calculator)

1 · Fundamentals and principle of the unit operation

R-101 turns liquid vinyl chloride monomer (VCM) into solid PVC grains. VCM is dispersed as droplets (typically 30–150 µm) in demineralised water by the agitator and held apart by a suspending agent (PVA). An oil-soluble peroxide initiator dissolves in the droplets, so each droplet is a small bulk-polymerisation reactor and the water around it carries the heat to the walls. PVC does not dissolve in its own monomer: it precipitates inside the droplet as a gel swollen with VCM, and the droplet becomes a porous grain. Six pieces of physics decide how the reactor behaves and how it must be designed.

1.1 Initiation: the peroxide decomposes at a rate set by temperature

Radicals come from the first-order decomposition of the initiator: dI/dt = −kdI, with kd = ln 2 / t½ at 57 °C, corrected with an activation energy Ea = 120 kJ/mol:

kd(T) = (ln 2 / t½,57) · exp[ −(Ea/R)(1/T − 1/330.15 K) ]

R-101 uses a pair: a fast initiator A (t½ 1.5 h at 57 °C) that starts the batch, and a slow initiator B (t½ 12 h) that is still there when A is used up. The radical flux is R = Σ kd,i Ii. Worked numbers are in the table below ().

1.2 Rate of polymerisation, heat release and the gel effect

For free-radical polymerisation with bimolecular termination the rate is proportional to the square root of the radical flux. The model lumps it as

rp = kX(T) · M0 · √(R/Rref) · g(X)    [kg PVC/s],    Qrx = rp · ΔHp    (ΔHp = 71 kJ/mol = 1136 kJ/kg)

  • Gel (Trommsdorff) effect: in the swollen PVC gel the growing chains can hardly meet to terminate, so the rate climbs as conversion rises: g = 1 + Q·X with Q = 5 while a free monomer phase exists.
  • End of the free monomer at Xf = 0.72: the gel holds 28 wt % VCM at saturation; once all the monomer is inside the gel (X > Xf) the monomer concentration in the gel falls and so does g. The heat release therefore peaks near X ≈ 0.72 and then falls away.
  • Temperature sensitivity: kX has 25 kJ/mol and √kd contributes 120/2 = 60 kJ/mol, so the overall activation energy is ≈ 85 kJ/mol: the heat release rises by per kelvin. This is the root of every runaway question on this unit (1.8).

1.3 Batch mass balance

Nothing leaves during the reaction except a little inert gas at the vent, so the balance is simply dmPVC/dt = rp, mVCM = M0 − mPVC, conversion X = mPVC/M0. PVC (1400 kg/m³) is much denser than liquid VCM (844 kg/m³ at 57 °C), so the batch shrinks as it converts; LIC-100 replaces the volume with injection water (FIC-103) to keep the jacket wetted.

1.4 Pressure: a vapour-pressure reactor

R-101 has no pressure controller. While free liquid monomer exists the pressure is fixed by the temperature:

P = aVCM · PsatVCM(T) + Psatwater(T) + pinerts,    aVCM = 1 for X < Xf

Above Xf the monomer activity in the gel follows Flory–Huggins, ln a = ln φ + (1 − φ) + χ(1 − φ)², with χ fitted so that a = 1 at 28 wt % VCM in the gel (φ = volume fraction of VCM in the gel). The activity, and with it the pressure, falls as the gel dries out. This fall is the batch end-point signal (PD-100).

1.5 Heat removal: three sinks in parallel

  • Jacket (tempered-water loop): Qj = U A (T − Tj,mean). P-101A circulates 130 kg/s round the jacket; TIC-110 injects cold CW (TV-110B) or LP steam (TV-110A) into the loop, and the same mass of warm water spills to CW return. The loop energy balance Qj = ṁloopcp(Tout − Tin) keeps the jacket rise small (≈ 2.7 K), so the whole wall sees nearly the same temperature. U falls as the slurry thickens (model: U = 0.75 (1 − 0.15 X) kW/m² K) and with any polymer film on the wall.
  • Cooling baffles (four, on once-through CW, FIC-120): a small exchanger with NTU = UA/(ṁcp) ≈ 0.19, so ε = 1 − e−NTU ≈ 0.17 and Qb = ε ṁcp(T − TCW) ≈ 0.4 MW whatever the batch does.
  • Reflux condenser E-101: VCM boils off the slurry, condenses on CW-cooled tubes and runs back. The condensing side is at the VCM saturation temperature, so Qc = ṁCWcp(1 − e−NTU)(Tcond − TCW). Its weakness: inert gas (N₂, air left after evacuation) is carried to the tubes and collects there, blanketing part of the surface (model: UA = 130 kW/K × (1 − b), b the blanketed fraction). HIC-135 vents inerts to VCM recovery.

1.6 K-value (molecular weight) is set by temperature

In VCM polymerisation the chain length is limited by chain transfer to monomer, not by the initiator, and chain transfer rises faster with temperature than propagation. The grade (K-value, a viscosity measure of molecular weight) is therefore fixed almost only by the reaction temperature; the model uses K = 67 − 0.62 (T − 57), about −0.6 K-units per °C. The specification 66–68 corresponds to . This is why the temperature set point is not an operating choice but a product specification: a faster batch is never made by running hotter.

1.7 Why a reflux condenser and a jacket both? Scale

Heat released grows with volume (∝ D³) while jacket area grows with D². At 140 m³ the jacket alone carries about 1.4 MW at 50 % CW valve and at most ≈ 1.6 MW with TV-110B wide open (section 5) — well under the 3.4 MW peak. The reflux condenser adds area that does not depend on the vessel wall; it is the usual answer for large PVC reactors.

1.8 Runaway: heat generation against heat removal (Semenov)

Heat generation rises exponentially with temperature; heat removal by coolant at a fixed temperature rises only linearly. The operating point is stable on its own only if the removal line is steeper than the generation curve: dQrem/dT > dQgen/dT. Equivalently, with a fixed coolant the reactor may run no more than about RT²/E above the coolant.

3 · Setting the operating conditions (การกำหนดสภาวะในการทำงาน)

A batch reactor has two kinds of conditions: recipe values fixed before the batch (charges, initiator, level) and running values held by the control system while it reacts (temperature, cooling split). Pressure is neither: it follows from temperature and composition. Each condition is chosen from a product or process requirement, then checked against an equipment limit. Limits below are read from the page's alarm table and trip settings.

Order in which the conditions are set during a batch

  1. Cooling ready first: jacket circulation (P-101A) and baffle water (FIC-120, 80 m³/h) before anything is charged.
  2. Evacuate (XV-109) below 0.05 bar a: oxygen inhibits the start, and every mole of inert gas later blankets E-101 and adds pressure.
  3. Recipe charges: water with PVA (FQI-101 preset), start M-101 when the lower impeller is covered, then VCM (FQI-102 preset). The charge ratio and the level are now fixed.
  4. Temperature: heat up on steam (TIC-110 split range, TV-110A), then TIC-100 in AUTO at 57 °C with TIC-110 in CAS.
  5. Initiator at 54–57 °C (XV-103): reaction time starts; the dose now decides the heat-release curve.
  6. Level: LIC-100 AUTO at 83 % with FIC-103 in CAS to follow the shrinkage.
  7. Heat-removal split: E-101 through VPC-130 → FIC-130 once conversion allows (anti-foam limit), inerts vented with HIC-135; TV-110B then stays near its 50 % set point.
  8. End point: PD-100 reaches the drop set point → short-stop, degas, discharge.

Operating window

From reference batches run on the model (full batch from the start of reaction, noise off). The dose is the initiator charge relative to the recipe (both initiators scaled).

4 · Conceptual design

4.1 Design basis

4.2 Design decisions

DecisionOptionsChoice for R-101Reason
Number and size of reactorsFew large (100–200 m³) · many small (25–60 m³)4 × 140 m³ batch reactorsLarge vessels cut labour, cleaning and cost per tonne; four reactors staggered in time give an almost steady flow to stripping and recovery and let one be cleaned or repaired while three run. Above ≈ 150–200 m³ the wall area per m³ becomes too small for the heat release unless much more condenser is added (section 5).
Split of heat removalJacket only · jacket + internal coils · jacket + baffles · + reflux condenserJacket ≈ 40 %, baffles ≈ 12 %, E-101 ≈ 48 % at the peakThe jacket is limited by wall area; coils foul with polymer and are hard to clean; cooled baffles are needed anyway for mixing and add ≈ 0.4 MW; E-101 takes the rest.
Reflux condenserNo · yesYes, vertical, CW-cooledIts area is independent of the vessel wall and it removes heat at the VCM condensing temperature. Costs: foam carry-over early in the batch (limited by the anti-foam clamp), fouling, and blanketing by inerts (vent HIC-135).
InitiatorSingle initiator · fast + slow pair · continuous dosingFast (1.5 h) + slow (12 h) pair, charged onceA single fast initiator gives an early heat peak and a dying end; a single slow one gives a sharp late peak with the gel effect. The pair flattens the heat release so the peak (≈ 1.3 × average) fits the cooling for a 5.3 h reaction.
Water charge temperatureCold water + long steam heat-up · hot-water chargeWater at 55 °CMost of the sensible heat arrives with the water, so the steam heat-up is short (≈ 20 min) and the cycle shorter.
Temperature control structureReactor T → CW valve · reactor T → jacket inlet T (cascade) · + valve-position control of E-101TIC-100 → TIC-110 cascade with split range steam/CW; VPC-130 → FIC-130The cascade removes loop disturbances before they reach the reactor; the split range gives one handle for heat-up and cooling; VPC-130 hands the slowly rising load to E-101 so the jacket always keeps margin both ways.
PressureControlled · floatingFloating (a result), alarmed and trippedPressure is the VCM vapour pressure: a vent control would throw monomer away. It is watched as a check on temperature and inerts and as the end-point signal.
Stopping the reactionCooling only · short-stop injection · dumpShort-stop pot XV-104 (N₂-driven) by operator and SISCooling cannot beat a runaway once the jacket and E-101 are saturated; a short-stop kills the radicals within a minute if the agitator mixes it.
Relief and emergency ventPSV only · PSV + emergency vent · rupture discPSV-100 at 15 bar g + ESD vent XV-108, both to a closed dump/vent systemVCM is toxic and flammable: no release to atmosphere. The PSV is the last layer; the SIS (TSHH-101, PSHH-101, XS-101, FSLL-110) acts well below it.
Safety instrumented functionsShared or independent sensorsTE-101 and PT-101 independent of TE-100 and PT-100A failed control element must not disable its own protection.

4.3 Design sequence

  1. Production basis: capacity, hours, grade (→ temperature 57 °C), number of reactors, reaction and non-reaction times → batch size (section 5 steps 1–2).
  2. Recipe: conversion at the end point, water ratio → VCM and water charges.
  3. Vessel: liquid volume at temperature, fill level (vapour space for boil-up and foam) → volume, L/D → diameter and length; check shrinkage and injection water.
  4. Kinetics: initiator pair and dose → heat-release curve, peak / average ratio (from a batch simulation or pilot data).
  5. Heat removal at the peak: jacket (area, U, loop flow, CW), baffles, and the remainder on the reflux condenser; check the total with every handle wide open against the peak, with margin.
  6. Reflux condenser: duty, CW rise, LMTD, UA with an inert allowance, area; vent sizing.
  7. Agitation: power per volume for the grain size, motor, seal.
  8. Pressure and relief: operating pressure from vapour pressure at the hottest grade, design pressure with margin, PSV set and runaway relief case, SIS trips between operating and PSV.
  9. Control and safety: loops, split range, VPC, sequence, SIS; then vendor data sheets.

Change any input; results update immediately. Defaults reproduce R-101. The column "Simulator" shows the model value (reference batch, design state or model constant) for comparison. ✓ / ✗ checks compare with the page's own alarms and trips, the simulator, or typical practice (labelled).

Assumptions and limits of this sizing

  • Liquid volume from the charges at reaction temperature (water ρ(T), VCM 947 − 1.8 T kg/m³); the ≈ 0.4 t of VCM in the vapour space is ignored (the model's start-of-reaction volume is 0.3 % smaller).
  • Vessel with 2:1 elliptical heads; the fill level is a fraction of the total inside height; the jacket covers the bottom head (area 1.084 D²) and the chosen share of the straight side.
  • The peak heat release is the average × a peak factor taken from the model's reference batch (1.32 with the fast + slow initiator pair). A different initiator system needs its own batch simulation.
  • Jacket: direct-injection loop with the model's effective relation Q = UA(T − TCW) / [1 + (UA/ṁcp)(1/e − ½)], e = CW injected / (loop + CW); U at the peak = U0(1 − 0.15 X).
  • E-101: condensing at the VCM saturation temperature − 0.5 K, counter-current LMTD; the blanketing allowance covers the inert fraction seen in the reference batch (≈ 10–12 %). E-101 U is assumed (the model uses a lumped UA).
  • Design pressure: typical practice, the larger of 1.1 × and + 1.7 bar above the maximum operating pressure (vapour pressure at the hottest grade + water + inerts). Relief for a runaway (two-phase, DIERS) needs a dynamic study; not covered here.
  • Guidelines quoted as "typical" (L/D, P/V, cooling margin) are common practice, not a vendor rating.

2 · The block flow diagram

Batch order: water and PVA (1) → VCM (2) → heat-up with steam into the jacket loop (12) → initiator (3) → reaction, with VCM boiling up to E-101 and running back (5/6) and shrinkage water (4) → end point → short-stop (16) → degassing (8) → slurry to D-102 (9). Streams 5–7 and 10–15 are rates or pressures; 1–4, 8, 9 and 16 are amounts per batch. Dashed blocks are outside this OTS.

3 · What goes in and out of each block

4 · Stream table (design and now)

From the Process tab's streamRows(). Per-batch amounts at design are the recipe and the reference batch; rates are the design state at 2.0 h. A batch is never steady, so Now differs from Design as the batch moves on even without any upset.

5 · Boundary balances

Draw a boundary round a block and count what crosses it. Each balance is computed from the model's states; the last three duties are also computed the way the DCS does it (flow × cp × ΔT from measured values), so the two ways can be compared. A row turns red only when its difference moves more than 2 points from its value at design.

6 · From BFD to PFD

  • Each block becomes equipment with a tag: "R-101" stays one block, "Jacket loop" becomes P-101A/B with the steam and CW injection valves, "VCM recovery" becomes the gasholder D-106 and compressor C-101, "Stripper, dryer" becomes T-201, S-201 and D-201.
  • Streams get their own PFD numbers (Turton style) and flags with flow, temperature and pressure where the model gives them; the PFD tab shows each flag beside its BFD number.
  • Control valves on the main streams appear (FV-101, FV-102, TV-110A/B, the vent and degassing valves); instruments, trips and manual valves wait for the P&ID.
  • Utilities (CW, LP steam, N₂) are drawn where they enter, not as blocks.

1 · What a PFD adds to the BFD

  • Equipment instead of blocks: every major item with its tag and a symbol in proportion to the real item (R-101 140 m³, the 1.25 bar a gasholder, the recovery compressor, the slurry pump).
  • Its own stream numbers (1–30) with flags (mass flow, temperature, pressure) where the heat and mass balance gives them.
  • The main control valves on charges, vents and the jacket utilities, and the utilities where they enter (CW, LP steam, N₂).
  • The plant around the reactor: vacuum pump, emergency vent tank, recovery, blowdown tank, and the shared stripper, centrifuge and dryer as one line-up.

3 · Equipment list

4 · Flags beside the model

The PFD numbers its own streams (Turton), which differ from the BFD and Process-tab numbers; the matching BFD number is in brackets. Design = the design state 2.0 h into the reaction (charge rates are the FIC set points); Now = the running simulator.

5 · Reading the PFD

  • Two fluids are never mixed except where the process mixes them: CW and LP steam are injected into the jacket loop on purpose (direct injection), but jacket water never meets the slurry; the reflux condenser keeps VCM and CW apart.
  • What goes in comes out: per batch, water + VCM charged leave as slurry to D-102 plus VCM to recovery; check it on the BFD tab's boundary balances.
  • Pressure falls along each path: VCM 12 bar g at P-103 → 8.6 bar g in R-101 → 0.24 bar g at the gasholder; water 5 bar g header into the reactor only before the VCM goes in (the reactor is then near vacuum or atmospheric).
  • One recycle: unreacted and stripped VCM goes back to TK-100 through C-101 (stream 17); there is no recycle inside the reactor batch other than the reflux 10 → 12.
  • Batch plant: most streams flow only in one step of the cycle, so a flag is a rate during that step, not a steady flow.

6 · What the P&ID adds

  • Every instrument and loop (TIC-100 → TIC-110 split range, VPC-130 → FIC-130, LIC-100 → FIC-103), the trips (TSHH-101, PSHH-101, XS-101, FSLL-110, LSHH-100) and their final elements.
  • On/off valves XV-101 … XV-109 and their fail positions, manual block valves, check valves, drains and vents, line numbers and sizes.
  • Relief: PSV-100 at 15 bar g and the emergency vent path to D-103.
  • See the P&ID tab: the screen drawing used by the DCS console, and the EPC sheets PVC-PID-001 and PVC-PID-002 below it.

Follows the course lecture Operating Windows (after T. Marlin's Process Operability class materials). Every window on this tab was computed on copies of this simulator's own model: 672 full batches for the Type II/III maps, 357 open-loop runs for Type I, 24 recipe-charge batches and the runs behind the capacity charts, with the SIS switched off in the copies so the limits can be seen rather than cut short. The live batch is never touched. Limits come from the page's alarms (ALM), the SIS set points (K), valve ranges and the grade specification; limits marked "assumed" are for teaching.

1 Batch operability · 2 Variability · 3 Bounds and IOW · 4 Worst case and point check · 5 Capacity and turndown · 6 Type I window · 7 Type II and III window · 8 Monte Carlo · 9 Manipulated variables · 10 Limitations

1 · Operability, and what a window means for a batch

Process operability means the plant has the capacity and flexibility to reach a range of operating conditions safely, reliably, profitably, with good dynamic performance and product quality. The operating window is the set of conditions for which every controlled variable can be held at its set point and no limit is broken. It is shaped by four things.

The adaptation to a batch reactor. The lecture's windows are steady-state: a point either can be held or not. R-101 never lines out. Its "operating point" is a trajectory from the initiator charge to the PD-100 end point, and the heat release climbs to its peak (≈ 3.4 MW at X ≈ 0.72, the gel effect) before it collapses. So on this tab a batch is feasible when every bound holds over the whole batch: its worst value, wherever in the batch it happens, must be inside the limit. The tightest point of the trajectory is usually the heat-release peak, but not always: an early excess of heat meets a condenser that is still held back by its anti-foam limit. A throughput bound (reaction time) replaces the steady-state production rate, and the handles that set the rate are the recipe charge and the initiator dose.

The variables of R-101 during the reaction

ClassVariable (tag)At the design state (2.0 h)Why it is in this class

2 · Variability: the design basis the window must cover

"The abnormal is normal." A window is only as good as the list of changes it was sized for. The five sources of variability, written as a design-basis memorandum for R-101 (ranges are the ones swept on this tab; frequencies are teaching values):

SourceWhat changes on R-101Range used hereHow oftenCovered by

A single human error must not cause an unsafe condition and must not stay undetected. That is why the fast bounds of part 3 carry alarms and, where the damage is quick, trips on independent elements (TE-101, PT-101).

3 · Bounds and the integrity operating window

The bounds are the frame of the window. A hard bound must not be crossed (trip set points, relief, the vessel); a soft bound can be crossed for a while (alarms, quality); a capacity bound is a handle at the end of its travel; the CV bound is the control objective itself. For a batch each bound is evaluated on its worst value over the batch:

IdBoundSourceKindHow it is evaluated over a batch

Live margins: the batch on the plant now against the design state

Margin now ÷ margin at the design state (2.0 h into the reference batch). Values are what the DCS shows (controller outputs, not field valve positions). Updated live.

BoundKindLimitDesignNowMargin now ÷ design

Reading the ladder. Inside the target range the batch makes the grade. Between the target and the alarm it is still safe, but the product or the margin is being spent. Past the alarm the operator must act; at the trip the SIS short-stops the batch; relief and the vessel design are the last line. The live value is the arrow.

4 · Design for the worst case, and a live point check

Equipment is sized for the worst case of the variability it must handle: for a heat sink (Q = U A ΔT) that is the highest heat release with the warmest cooling water and the most fouling. Each piece of R-101's heat-removal train has its own worst case. Pick one, or set your own batch, and the page runs a full batch on a copy of the model (TIC-100 cascade, VPC-130, the anti-foam limit, SIS off so every limit is seen) and checks every bound. A run takes about a second.

5 · Capacity and turndown

A small reactor train that only just meets the design batch is cheap but has no window; a large one has a window but costs capital. The capacity must keep the batch safe and on grade for the base case and the frequently occurring variability; a slower batch is acceptable in rare cases; stop (short-stop) for the extreme ones.

5a · The heat sinks in series with the heat release

Each sink's largest possible removal at 57 °C, from the model's own relations (jacket: tempered loop with TV-110B wide open, Q = UA(T − Tjm) with the loop balance; baffles: FV-120 wide open; E-101: effectiveness–NTU with the condensing temperature from the VCM activity, up to the anti-foam limit and up to 540 m³/h), evaluated on the states of the reference batch and plotted against conversion together with the heat released by batches of several initiator doses.

Rule of thumbWhat it saysThe R-101 modelWhy they differ

5b · Turndown: the recipe range each bound allows ("series plant")

The batch's range is the overlap of what every bound allows, so it is always smaller than any single element's. Dose ranges come from the Type III column at the chosen CW temperature (part 7 grid, clean equipment, grade 57 °C); charge ranges from 12 full batches at dose 1.0. Ends are interpolated between grid points; a bound that is met over the whole swept range shows an arrow.

6 · Type I window: what the two heat-removal handles can reach

The lecture writes the model as y = A u + B d + C (y controlled, u manipulated, d disturbances) and poses three problems:

TypeGivenFindOn R-101
Iu over its range; d fixedachievable yAt the design instant (2.0 h, X ≈ 0.26): TIC-110 output (steam 0–50 %, jacket CW 50–100 %) × FIC-130 flow 0–540 m³/h held fixed, TIC-100 and VPC-130 in manual → reactor temperature over the next 40 min
IIy at set point (whole batch); d over its rangeu neededTIC-100 at 57 °C with the cascade and VPC-130; initiator dose 0.5–1.8 × CW supply 26–40 °C → peak TV-110B, peak E-101 water, reaction time
IIIy at set point; u within ranged that can be absorbedthe dose and CW combinations for which every bound of part 3 holds over the whole batch, and which bound stops the rest

At a steady state the balance is Qreleased = Qremoved. For an exothermic reactor that balance is open-loop unstable: a slightly hotter batch releases more heat (Arrhenius, ≈ 85 kJ/mol overall), which heats it further. With both handles frozen, only settings on a thin line keep 57 ± 0.5 °C, and only for a while, because the release also grows with conversion.

outlined cells = within 57 ± 0.5 °C for the whole horizon

7 · Type II and Type III: the disturbances a batch can absorb

Now TIC-100 holds its set point through the cascade, VPC-130 moves the E-101 water to keep TV-110B near 50 %, and the disturbances move between batches. Type II reads what the handles needed over the batch; Type III keeps the batches for which every bound held and colours the rest by the bound that failed first (root cause first: capacity, then hard, soft, specification, throughput, and only then "temperature not held").

8 · Monte Carlo operating window

The lecture's recipe: (1) simulate the base case, (2) replace the uncertain inputs by samples from their distributions and repeat, (3) mark each sample feasible or not against every bound, (4) report the fraction. Here the normalised margin (smallest slack ÷ scale over all bounds) is interpolated in the part-7 grids: dose and CW supply bilinearly, wall fouling linearly between the clean, −22 % and −45 % planes.

9 · Manipulated variables: enough, strong, independent, fast

With n adjustable handles and m variables to hold: n = m gives a finite window with each point exactly specified; n < m gives no window and is not an acceptable design; n > m leaves freedom that can be used (here: to keep a valve mid-range).

    1 What flexibility is · 2 How many · 3 Where · 4 Fluid flow · 5 Heat transfer · 6 Production rate · 7 Heat-removal strategies · 8 How much · 9 Recommendations

    1 · What flexibility is

    Flexibility is the ability of a plant to operate reliably across a wide range of rates and conditions without losing quantity or quality. Some controlled variables are held at their set points while disturbances arrive; flexibility is what lets us steer the process after the equipment has been built.

    Without flexibility a batch passes every disturbance on to its temperature, hence to the K-value, the pressure and in the end the SIS. With flexibility the heat that the batch releases is taken away wherever there is room: jacket, baffles or condenser.

    How it is provided on R-101

    • Spare capacity: TV-110B travel, E-101 area and water, the spare jacket pump P-101B.
    • Adjustable utility flows: CW injection into the jacket loop, LP steam, baffle CW, E-101 CW.
    • Mixing instead of a by-pass: the jacket inlet temperature is set by injecting CW (or steam) into a constant circulation, so the jacket flow and its film coefficient never change.

    Four design questions: how many handles, where, which tools (valves, pumps, mixing), and how much capacity.

    The flexibility register of R-101

    "At design" is the design state, 2.0 h into the reaction; "at the peak" is the reference batch at X ≈ 0.70, just before the heat-release peak. Duties from the model's heat-transfer relations at 57 °C and 32 °C CW.

    HandleWhat it adjustsKind of flexibilityAt designAt the peakSpare at the peakStatus

    2 · How many handles? Degrees of freedom

    A successful design needs number of adjustable valves ≥ number of variables to be held. The maximum number of controlled variables equals the degrees of freedom; the minimum number of handles equals the number of variables we insist on.

    Variable R-101 must holdWhyHandle used

    3 · Where? Causal paths from each handle

    Each held variable needs a handle with an independent causal path to it. Interaction is allowed as long as every desired point can still be reached. The lecture's three cases on R-101:

    Open-loop effect of +5 % on each handle, all loops in manual, 5 minutes, run on the model (the numbers behind the causal map). Changes are relative to the same 5 minutes with nothing moved.

    Two heat-removal handles for one temperature: why VPC-130 exists

    Share an extra duty between the sinks. Ask for more heat removal at the design state and the page solves the model's own relations for the move each sink would need on its own:

    4 · Flexibility for fluid flow

    For liquids the flow settles where the pump's pressure rise equals the losses: F = √(ΔP / ((fL/D + Kvalve + ΣKj) ρ/2g)). Only the valve term (or the number and speed of pumps) is adjustable. Three flows on R-101 show three kinds of flexibility.

    4a · The jacket loop: constant circulation, one spare pump (illustration)

    Illustration: head 25 m at the design 473 m³/h is assumed, and the pump curve is chosen so that two pumps in parallel give +10 % flow, the ratio the model uses (K.Fc × 1.1). The simulator itself does not compute loop hydraulics: it holds the circulation at 130 kg/s per running pump.

    4b · TV-110B: CW injected into the loop, and the duty it buys (the model's own equations)

    The CW flow is linear in the valve (the model: 110 kg/s at 100 %, constant header ΔP), but the duty is not. Injected CW displaces warm loop water, so the jacket inlet falls as Tji = Tjo − Fcw(Tjo − Tcw)/(Fc + Fcw), and the duty is capped by the wall: Q = UA(T − Tjm). Once the inlet is close to the CW temperature, more valve gives almost nothing.

    4c · FV-130: E-101 cooling water and its duty (the model's own equations)

    Q = Cc(1 − e−UA/Cc)(Tcond − Tcw): at low flow the water leaves near the condensing temperature (flow-limited, strong gain); at high flow the area limits (weak gain). The anti-foam clamp caps the flow early in the batch, the 540 m³/h valve later.

    5 · Flexibility for heat transfer

    Q = U A ΔT: flexibility can act on U (a flow changes the film coefficient), on A (level, active area) or on ΔT (a utility's temperature or flow, mixing). Numbers at the design state from the model:

    What fouling and inerts do to the capacity at the peak

    Spare in each sink across the batch (reference batch, 32 °C CW)

    Bars: duty each sink carried in the reference run (solid) and what it could have carried at 57 °C (pale; E-101 up to its anti-foam limit), at eight points along the batch.

    6 · Flexibility for production rate

    A batch reactor has no feed rate. Its production rate is PVC per batch ÷ cycle time, and the handles are the recipe charge (batch size) and the initiator dose (how fast the reaction step runs). Both are set before the batch; during it every other flow follows automatically: TIC-100 → TIC-110 → TV-110A/B, VPC-130 → FIC-130, LIC-100 → FIC-103.

    Guiding principleR-101

    HAZID · Hazard identification of the R-101 area

    A plant-level, checklist-driven identification of the major hazards around the PVC reactor R-101 — its VCM store, charge preparation, heat removal, recovery, blowdown and the downstream units — done before (and wider than) the detailed HAZOP. It uses the same example risk matrix as the HAZOP tab; a real study uses the owner's matrix, a multidisciplinary team and the site plot plan.

    1 What HAZID is · 2 Method · 3 PFD and study areas · 4 Guideword checklist · 5 Hazard register · 6 Major accident hazards · 7 From HAZID to HAZOP

    1 · What HAZID is and where it sits

    HAZID (hazard identification) is a structured brainstorm of what could go badly wrong across the whole facility, including its surroundings, people and environment. It is done early — concept and front-end design — with the PFD, the layout and the design basis, so that the major hazards shape the design before the details are fixed. It asks broad questions ("what hazards exist in the VCM store?"); HAZOP asks detailed ones ("what if the flow of cooling water to E-101 is less than intended?").

    HAZIDHAZOP
    WhenConcept / FEED, and before major changesDetailed design with the P&ID frozen; revalidation
    DrawingPFD, plot planP&ID, cause-and-effect (trip) chart, batch sequence
    BreakdownAreas / systemsNodes with one design intent (plus procedure nodes for a batch plant)
    PromptGuideword checklist by hazard category (natural, external, process, reactive chemistry, utilities, health, occupational, environment, operations, people)Guide word × parameter (NO flow, MORE temperature, BEFORE in the sequence …)
    ScopeProcess and non-process hazards, site and surroundingsProcess deviations and operability
    OutputHazard register, list of major accident hazards (MAH), studies to do next (HAZOP, fire and explosion, dust, SIL, layout, occupational exposure)Worksheets and recommendations per deviation
    ReferenceISO 17776 (major accident hazard management in design; HAZID and its checklist); company HSE practiceIEC 61882

    2 · Method

    1. Define scope and basis: R-101 (one of four 140 m³ reactors) with the VCM store and charge pump, water/PVA/initiator/short-stop preparation, the jacket loop and cooling water, E-101 and the vents, VCM recovery, the emergency vent and blowdown, and — as blocks — the shared stripping, dewatering and drying units; site conditions; risk matrix.
    2. Divide the plant into areas on the PFD (section 3).
    3. Apply the guideword checklist to each area (section 4): for every category ask whether the hazard exists here, what could release it (cause / threat) and what would follow (top event and outcome).
    4. Record the existing controls, split into prevention (stops the top event) and mitigation (limits the outcome), as in a bow-tie.
    5. Rank the risk (S × L with the controls) and flag major accident hazards (MAH): events that could cause multiple fatalities, major damage or a major environmental release.
    6. Assign actions and further studies: design changes, HAZOP nodes, fire and explosion analysis, dust study, SIL assessment, layout review, occupational-exposure programme.
    What makes a PVC reactor different from a continuous unit: the hazard moves with the batch phase. Air must be out before VCM goes in; the heat release is small at initiation and peaks near 72 % conversion (gel effect); the pressure is set by the VCM vapour pressure until the free monomer is gone; and at the end VCM must be recovered before the reactor is discharged or opened. A HAZID of a batch plant therefore asks each question for each phase, not only for the steady state.

The coloured markers are the HAZID areas, coloured by the highest risk found there; click one to filter the register.

    Twelve categories, each with the prompts used on this plant and the hazards it produced. The "reactive chemistry" row takes the place of the combustion row used for a fired heater.

    5 · Hazard register

    S and L use the risk matrix in the HAZOP tab (section 5): S is the worst credible outcome, L its likelihood with the existing controls. Scenarios that the HAZOP also ranks carry the same S × L (table below).

    6 · Major accident hazards and what they lead to

      7 · From HAZID to HAZOP and other studies

      • Every process MAH is examined in detail in the HAZOP tab: runaway → nodes N3 (initiator), N4 (reactor), N5 (jacket and CW), N7 (E-101) and N8 (short-stop and relief); VCM releases → N2 and N9; peroxide decomposition → N3; procedures (evacuation, initiation, opening the reactor) → N10.
      • The trips that stop a runaway (TSHH-101, PSHH-101, XS-101, FSLL-110 → short-stop XV-104) go to LOPA and a SIL assessment (IEC 61511) — see the Safety layers and LOPA tabs.
      • The emergency relief (PSV-100, XV-108, D-103) goes to a runaway relief study with two-phase flow (DIERS method).
      • VCM fire and explosion hazards (HD-02, HD-03, HD-04, HD-11, HD-26, HD-28) go to a fire and explosion analysis, hazardous-area classification and a layout / separation check of the four-reactor building; PVC dust (HD-17) to a dust-explosion study.
      • VCM exposure (HD-18, HD-22, HD-31) goes to the occupational-exposure programme: opening criterion at the manway, closed-reactor cleaning, monitoring and health surveillance; confined space and burns (HD-10, HD-23) to the permit-to-work procedures.
      • The register is revisited when the design, the recipe or the initiator changes (management of change).

      1 · Control objectives (ต้องการควบคุมอะไร และเพราะอะไร)

      Control design starts from objectives, not from instruments. They are ranked: a lower objective is never met by giving up a higher one — for example, a batch is never made faster by running hotter, because that costs quality (K-value) and runaway margin.

      PriorityObjectiveVariable that shows itHow it is met on R-101

      2 Equipment protectionNo liquid-full reactor, no condenser fouling, pumps and agitator within limitsLI-100 / LSHH-100, TI-131, TI-132, JI-100, FI-110LIC-100 → FIC-103; LSHH-100 closes charges and injection; anti-foam limit on FIC-130; alarms
      3 Product qualityK-value 67 → temperature 57 ± 0.5 °C; no lumps; no foamTIC-100 (TE-100), KX-100, JI-100TIC-100 → TIC-110 cascade with split range; agitator always running; anti-foam clamp
      4 ThroughputShortest batch the cooling allowsXI-100, PD-100, reaction timeInitiator dose (recipe); cooling margin kept for the peak by VPC-130 → FIC-130; end point by PD-100
      5 Efficient operationLittle CW, steam and vented VCMCW total, TV-110A, FI-135VPC-130 uses E-101 only as much as needed; FIC-120 fixed; HIC-135 opened only when inerts collect

      2 · The feedback loop: parts and vocabulary

      TermMeaningExample on R-101

      Set point (SP)The value the CV should have.
      Errore = SP − PV (reverse action) or PV − SP (direct action), in % of the transmitter span.SP 57.0, PV 57.3 °C → e = −0.3 °C = −0.3 % of the 0–100 °C span

      In this simulator OUT is always shown as % open (for TIC-110, the split-range signal: 0–50 % opens TV-110A from 100 to 0 %, 50–100 % opens TV-110B from 0 to 100 %). With a fail-open valve the signal to the actuator is inverted in the field; the operator does not see that inversion.

      4 · Degrees of freedom (DOF)

      Why it matters. The degrees of freedom tell the designer how many variables can be held independently. Control more CVs than there are independent MVs and controllers fight over one valve; control fewer and some variable drifts wherever the disturbances push it.

      NDOF = Nvariables − Nindependent equations    and    NDOF = Ndisturbances (fixed by the surroundings) + Nmanipulated

      For control the useful count is the control DOF = number of independent manipulated variables: the independent valves, speeds and on/off devices on the P&ID.

      4.1 Handles on the R-101 P&ID

      Why TV-110A and TV-110B count as one handle. Both are driven by the single output of TIC-110 through a split range (0–50 % steam, 50–100 % CW), so they can never be moved independently and are never open together. Physically they change one thing — the net heat put into the jacket loop (steam in minus CW in) — and therefore one variable, the jacket inlet temperature. Two separate controllers on the two valves would fight: steam heating the loop while CW cools it, wasting both. The split range turns two valves into one DOF with a range from full heating to full cooling.

      4.2 DOF during the reaction (quasi-steady balance at the design point)

      Variables (15)Equations (10)
      T reactor · P · pI inerts · L level · Qrx · Qj · Qb · Qc · Tji · Tjo · u110 (split-range signal) · v120 · v130 · v103 · h135 1 Reactor energy balance: Qrx + Pagitator = Qj + Qb + Qc (+ injection water)
      2 Kinetics: Qrx = f(T, X, initiator) — X and initiator are the batch state at this moment
      3 Pressure: P = a Psat(T) + Psatw(T) + pI
      4 Inert balance: vent (h135) = in-leakage → pI
      5 Volume balance: injection (v103) = shrinkage → dL/dt
      6 Jacket transfer: Qj = UA(T − (Tji + Tjo)/2)
      7 Jacket loop balance: Qj = ṁcp(Tjo − Tji)
      8 Injection mixing: Tji = f(Tjo, u110, TCW, steam)
      9 Baffles: Qb = f(v120, T, TCW)
      10 E-101: Qc = f(v130, T, pI blanketing, TCW)

      DOF = 15 − 10 = 5: exactly the five handles that are live during the reaction — the TV-110A/B split range, FV-120, FV-130, FV-103 and HV-135. (FV-101, FV-102 and HV-105 are isolated by XV-101, XV-102 and XV-105 while the batch reacts; the sequence uses them before and after.) CW temperature, steam pressure and the batch state are disturbances, not counted. Pressure is not among the free variables: equation 3 fixes it once T and pI are fixed, so R-101 cannot have a pressure controller as well as a temperature controller.

      DOF (handle)Used to fixByWhy this pairing
      TV-110A/B (split range)T (through Tji)TIC-100 → TIC-110 (auto, cascade)The only handle that can both heat and cool, with one sign over the whole range; acts on the wall next to the reaction mass.
      FV-130u110 (TV-110B demand) at 50 %VPC-130 → FIC-130 (auto, cascade)E-101 carries the bulk of the rising heat release slowly, so the fast jacket loop keeps margin both ways. A valve position is the CV here.
      FV-120Baffle water at 80 m³/hFIC-120 (auto)A fixed base load of ≈ 0.4 MW; small gain, not worth a temperature loop.
      FV-103LLIC-100 → FIC-103 (auto, cascade)Only water can replace the shrinkage; direct and one-signed.
      HV-135pI (E-101 unblanketed)Operator (manual), guided by TI-132Venting loses VCM; only needed now and then, so left in manual with an alarm.

      4.3 DOF of each loop

      • A feedback loop uses one DOF: it turns "valve position is free" into "CV = SP". The SP becomes the new free input, given by the operator or by a master controller.
      • Cascade, split range and limiters do not create DOF. TIC-100 and TIC-110 together still act through one handle (TV-110A/B); VPC-130 and FIC-130 through FV-130; LIC-100 and FIC-103 through FV-103. The anti-foam clamp only limits the FIC-130 set point.
      • A controller in MAN gives its DOF back to the operator (loop open). A saturated valve (0 or 100 %) loses its DOF: when TV-110B is at 100 % and E-101 is at its maximum, nothing holds the temperature any more — that is the moment to short-stop.
      • Two controllers must never move the same valve at the same time unless a selector or split range decides which acts.

      5 · The control loops on the P&ID

      Blue-green: cooling water; red: LP steam; blue: VCM; purple: VCM vapour; brown: vents. Dashed black: control signals; dashed red: SIS (independent elements). The table reads the tuning, set points and modes of the running session live.

      6 · How the loops were chosen for this P&ID (หลักการกำหนด control loop ตาม P&ID)

      1. Start from the objectives and the DOF. Five live handles during the reaction, so at most five fixed variables. Quality and safety need the temperature; the level protects the jacket; the rest is a choice of how to use the cooling.
      2. Pair each CV with the MV that affects it most directly, with one sign, over the whole range. The step tests below show that E-101 water moves the heat removal fastest and most per % of valve, yet the reactor temperature is paired with the jacket: only the split range can heat as well as cool (heat-up, slow periods), its sign never changes, and it acts on the wall of the batch. E-101's gain changes a lot (it falls at high flow, with inerts, and is clamped early in the batch against foam), so E-101 carries the slow bulk load instead.
      3. Use cascade for a fast inner disturbance. CW temperature, steam pressure and loop return temperature disturb the jacket inlet within seconds; TIC-110 removes them before the slow reactor sees them. The inner loop must be several times faster than the outer one.
      4. Put fast flow loops on the valves (FIC-101, -102, -103, -120, -130): they remove valve non-linearity and CW header-pressure changes in seconds.
      5. Keep a mid-range handle mid-range. A valve near 100 % has no margin for the next disturbance. VPC-130 holds TV-110B near 50 % by moving E-101: the jacket stays the fast trim, E-101 the slow bulk load. It must be much slower than TIC-100 or the two fight.
      6. Keep safety separate from control. TSHH-101 uses TE-101, not TE-100; PSHH-101 uses PT-101, not PT-100. A drifting control element must not disable its own trip.
      7. Choose fail positions for the safe state, independent of the action: cooling valves fail open, steam and every feed fail closed.
      8. Do not control what physics fixes. Pressure is the vapour pressure: controlling it would mean venting monomer. It is alarmed, tripped and used as the end-point signal.
      9. Leave rarely used, costly handles in manual with an alarm: HIC-135 (inert vent, TI-132 LO) and HIC-105 (degassing, after the short-stop).

      Pairing tests on the model (each handle's OUT +5 % in MAN, TIC-100 and VPC-130 in MAN, from the 2.0 h design state)

      StructurePrincipleUse it whenOn R-101
      Manual (open loop)The operator sets the valve; nothing corrects disturbances.The variable changes rarely, or automatic action would cost too much.Used: HIC-135 inert vent, HIC-105 degassing
      Single feedbackMeasure the CV, compare with SP, move the MV to remove the error. Corrects any disturbance, but only after it has moved the CV.Almost always the base layer.Used: FIC-120; the flow loops
      CascadeThe master sets the SP of a faster slave. The slave removes its own disturbances before they reach the master's CV. Slave 3–5 × faster (or more).A fast disturbance acts on the path from the valve to the CV.Used: TIC-100 → TIC-110; LIC-100 → FIC-103; VPC-130 → FIC-130
      Split rangeOne controller output drives two valves in sequence (0–50 % valve A, 50–100 % valve B).One CV needs two handles, e.g. heat and cool.Used: TIC-110 → TV-110A (steam) / TV-110B (CW)
      Valve-position control (VPC)A slow controller whose PV is another controller's output: it moves a second, slower handle so the first valve returns to a chosen position.A fast but small (or costly) handle plus a slow, large one.Used: VPC-130 holds TV-110B near 50 % with E-101 water
      RatioOne flow's SP = ratio × another (wild) flow.Blending, continuous feeds.Not used: the water : VCM ratio is fixed by the batch presets FQI-101 / FQI-102, not by a ratio controller
      FeedforwardMeasure a disturbance and move the MV before the CV changes, using a model; needs feedback trim.A large, measurable disturbance.Not used; possible upgrade: the calorimetric heat release (QI-100 / XI-100) as a bias on the TIC-110 set point or the E-101 water
      Override / selector (limiter)A selector passes the lower (or higher) of two signals so a constraint takes over when it is reached.Protect a constraint while normally controlling another CV.Used (as a limiter): FIC-130 SP = min(VPC-130 output, 12 m³/h per % XI-100) — the anti-foam clamp
      Batch sequence and interlocksDiscrete logic: presets, permissives, steps, end point; SIS trips on independent sensors drive to the safe state.Batch units; hazards that control cannot be trusted with.Used: FQI presets close XV-101 / XV-102; permissives for VCM and initiator; PD-100 end point; SIS: TSHH-101, PSHH-101, XS-101, FSLL-110 → short-stop; LSHH-100; ESD → XV-108

      8 · Control modes: P, PI and PID (แนวทางการควบคุม P, PI, PID)

      The simulator's controller (pid() in the model) uses the ideal PID form with signals in % of span, derivative on the measurement (filtered with Td/8), bumpless transfer and an anti-windup clamp:

      e = SP% − PV% (reverse) or PV% − SP% (direct),   OUT = Kc e + I + D,   dI/dt = Kc e / Ti,   D = ∓Kc Td dPV%/dt

      • Bumpless: when a loop goes to AUTO the integral starts at I = OUT − Kce − D, so OUT does not jump.
      • Anti-windup: if OUT would pass 0 or 100 %, it is clamped and the integral is reset so that OUT sits exactly on the limit; it leaves the limit as soon as the error changes sign.
      • P only (Ti = 0): the integral stays at its starting value (the bias), so any load change leaves an offset.
      • Cascade: while the slave is not in CAS the master tracks it (its OUT follows the slave SP), so switching back to CAS is bumpless.

      8.1 What each term does

      ModeActionGoodBadTypical use
      P (proportional)OUT change ∝ error now.Simple, immediate.Offset after a load change: e = Δload / (1 + KcK). High gain → oscillation. On an open-loop unstable process a gain that is too low cannot hold it at all.Averaging level control.
      PI (+ integral)Adds the accumulated error; keeps moving OUT until the error is zero.No offset for steps. The industrial default.Slower, overshoot if Ti is short; windup at a saturated valve; a steady lag behind a ramp (e = ramp × Ti/(KcK)) — important in a batch whose heat release keeps rising.Flow, pressure, most temperature and level loops.
      PID (+ derivative)Adds action ∝ rate of change of PV; anticipates.Faster, less overshoot on slow, lag-dominated loops with clean signals.Amplifies noise; derivative on error kicks on SP changes (hence derivative on PV).Slow temperature loops — TIC-100 uses Td = 120 s.

      8.2 Guidelines by loop type, and the R-101 tuning

      8.3 Tuning from a step test (FOPDT model)

      Put the loop in MAN, step OUT, record PV. Fit a first-order-plus-dead-time model G(s) = K e−θs/(τs + 1): K = ΔPV/ΔOUT (both in % of span); from the times to 28.3 % and 63.2 % of the final change, τ = 1.5 (t63 − t28), θ = t63 − τ. Then the lambda (IMC) PI rule with closed-loop time constant λ: Kc = τ / [K(λ + θ)], Ti = τ. A process that does not settle — an integrating or unstable one — has no final value: fit the initial slope K′ = (dPV/dt)/ΔOUT instead and use the SIMC rule for an integrating process, Kc = 1/[K′(λ + θ)], Ti = 4(λ + θ).

      A batch never sits still. Its heat release rises all the time, so each test below is run twice on copies of the model — with and without the step — and the difference is fitted.

      Things to try

      1. P leaves an offset, PI removes it. TIC-100, load "CW supply +3 °C", 30 min: P only ends about 0.15 °C below 57 °C; the simulator PI ends within 0.03 °C. With the initiator slug P only ends ≈ 0.07 °C high, PI ≈ 0.01 °C.
      2. An unstable process needs a minimum gain. TIC-100, initiator slug, 60 min, P only with Kc = 0.3: the temperature keeps rising and TSHH-101 trips the batch at about 53 min. Kc = 2 holds it with ≈ 0.55 °C offset; the simulator's 12 holds it within 0.1 °C. On a normal (self-regulating) loop a low gain is merely slow; here it is unsafe.
      3. Gain and speed. TIC-100, set-point step: 60 min: Kc 2 overshoots ≈ 0.17 °C and needs ≈ 28 min to settle within ±0.1 °C; Kc 12 (simulator) overshoots ≈ 0.06 °C and settles in ≈ 4 min.
      4. The slave. TIC-110, set-point step: the lambda preset (Kc ≈ 6, Ti ≈ 113 s) overshoots less than the simulator's 2 / 40 s; P only with Kc 2 stops ≈ 1.5 °C short of the new set point.
      5. A batch is a ramp. VPC-130, set-point step 50 → 40 %: with Ti 900 s the PV settles about 3.4 % above its set point because the heat release keeps rising; Ti 300 s cuts the lag to ≈ 1.2 %. P only leaves ≈ 14 %.
      6. Flow loops. FIC-130, set-point step: the lambda preset (Kc ≈ 1.1, Ti 3 s) settles in seconds without overshoot; Kc 2 with Ti 1 s overshoots ≈ 3.3 m³/h (14 % of the step).

      1 · Standard and method (IEC 61882)

      HAZOP is a structured, team-based examination of a defined system. Each part of the design is compared with its design intent; guide words combined with process parameters generate deviations; for each credible deviation the team records causes, consequences, existing safeguards and, where the risk is not acceptable, recommendations. It finds both hazards (harm to people, environment, assets) and operability problems (the batch cannot be made to grade or on time). For a batch reactor the intent changes with the phase, so the time-related guide words (EARLY, LATE, BEFORE, AFTER) and a procedure node matter as much as NO flow or MORE temperature.

      CCPS Guidelines for Process Safety in Batch Reaction Systems; DIERS methodologyRunaway scenarios, short-stop systems, emergency relief sizing with two-phase flow
      ISO 31000 / owner's risk matrixRisk criteria used to decide whether safeguards are adequate
      Thailand: Department of Industrial Works regulation on hazard identification, risk assessment and risk-management plans (B.E. 2543)Legal requirement to identify hazards (HAZOP is an accepted method) and to prepare risk-management plans for factories
      OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 (PSM), where applicable; occupational VCM standards (e.g. OSHA 1910.1017)Process hazard analysis for covered processes, revalidated at least every five years; VCM exposure control at opening and cleaning

      The four phases

      1. Definition: scope R-101 from the charge valves (water, VCM, initiator, short-stop) to XV-105 (recovery header) and XV-106 (to D-102), including the jacket loop, baffles, E-101 and its vent, the SIS and relief, and the batch procedures; excluded: TK-100 store internals, the recovery plant, D-102 onwards, the other three reactors (covered by the HAZID). Objectives, team, risk matrix.
      2. Preparation: collect the P&ID, PFD, design data, cause-and-effect (trip) chart, batch sequence and permissives, operating procedures, alarm list, datasheets; divide the plant into nodes; write each node's design intent; choose parameters and guide words.
      3. Examination: for each node → state the design intent → choose a parameter → apply each guide word → is the deviation meaningful? → causes → consequences assuming the safeguards fail → existing safeguards → rank the risk → recommend → next guide word. Record every meaningful deviation, including those with adequate safeguards ("full recording"), so the reasoning can be audited.
      4. Documentation and follow-up: worksheets, recommendation register with owners and dates, action close-out, and revalidation after changes (MOC) or periodically.

      2 · Team and documents

      RoleResponsibility
      HAZOP leader (chair)Independent of the design; runs the method, keeps the team on the node, decides when a deviation is covered
      Scribe (recorder)Writes the worksheet live, reads back recommendations
      Process engineer (designer)Design intent, recipe, heat balance, cooling capacity, relief basis
      Operations representativeHow batches are really run: charging, heat-up, end point, degassing, opening and cleaning
      Instrument / control engineerLoops, fail positions, batch sequence and permissives, SIS logic and trip independence
      Safety / risk engineerRisk matrix, LOPA follow-up, regulations, occupational VCM exposure
      Specialists as neededPolymerisation chemist (initiator, short-stop, gel effect), mechanical (agitator, seals), initiator supplier (SADT)

      Documents for this study: P&ID tab (PVC-PID-001 and -002), Process tab (stream table and duties), Design tab (limits and sizing), Control loop design tab, Workbook tab (alarm and trip list), Batch & SIS tab (permissives), the cold-start and end-of-batch procedures in the Exercises tab, and the HAZID tab (PFD-100).

      3 · Nodes

      A node is a part of the plant with one clear design intent. Boundaries are put where the intent changes (a charge valve, a pump, the reactor wall, a condenser, a relief device). A batch reactor also changes intent with time, so the procedures — evacuation, charging, initiation, end point and opening the reactor — get their own node N10.

      4 · Guide words and parameters

      Parameters used: flow, pressure, temperature, level, composition, agitation, heat transfer, measurement, control, utility, integrity (containment), safety system, and for procedures: sequence, timing, evacuation, charging, initiation, end point, opening, recipe, restart. A deviation is recorded only if it is physically meaningful ("REVERSE temperature" is not).

      5 · Risk matrix (example for teaching)

      Numbers in brackets: how many deviations of this study fall in the cell. Risk = S × L (the same matrix ranks the HAZID register).

      SSeverity (worst credible consequence, no credit for safeguards)
      1No injury; batch delayed
      2First aid; off-grade batch; small contained release
      3Lost-time injury; reactor out for days (lumps, fouling); local release
      4Permanent disability or single fatality; VCM release with fire; serious occupational exposure
      5Multiple fatalities; runaway with vessel rupture or vapour-cloud explosion; escalation to the other reactors
      LLikelihood with the existing safeguards
      1Remote: not expected in the life of the plant (< 10⁻⁴ /y)
      2Unlikely: known in industry (10⁻⁴–10⁻³ /y)
      3Possible: could happen in the plant life (10⁻³–10⁻² /y)
      4Likely: several times in the plant life (10⁻²–10⁻¹ /y)
      5Frequent: yearly or more

      1–4 Low acceptable · 5–9 Medium reduce if practicable (ALARP), review safeguards · 10–16 High recommendation required, consider LOPA · 20–25 Very high not acceptable, act before operation

      6 · HAZOP worksheets (node by node)

      Consequences are written assuming the safeguards fail (worst credible case). S ranks that consequence; L ranks its likelihood with the listed safeguards working as designed. Safeguard settings are read from the simulator's own trip and alarm tables.

      7 · Coverage check: guide words applied in each node

      A dot means that guide word gave no meaningful deviation for any parameter in the node (it was still considered). EARLY / LATE / BEFORE / AFTER apply mainly to the charge nodes, the end of batch (N9) and the procedure node N10.

      8 · Recommendation register

      9 · Dynamic check of selected deviations on the simulator

      A conventional HAZOP judges consequences qualitatively. Here selected deviations are run on copies of the R-101 model from the 2.0 h design state (X ≈ 26 %) with the existing safeguards active — alarms, SIS trips, controllers in their normal modes — and no operator action, for 30 min. The result shows whether the safeguards act before harm and how much time the operator has. Alarms are checked every second with the page's alarm table; the live simulator is not touched.

      What the runs tell the HAZOP team

        10 · Follow-up and close-out

        • Each recommendation gets an owner and a due date; the owner answers accepted and done, accepted with an alternative (with justification) or rejected (with a justification agreed by the HAZOP leader and the plant manager). The register in section 8 is the tracking list.
        • High scenarios whose protection relies on instrumented trips (runaway by loss of cooling, agitation or by initiator overcharge) go to LOPA to set the SIL of the short-stop function (IEC 61511) — see the Safety layers and LOPA tabs.
        • The emergency relief basis (PSV-100, XV-108, D-103) is confirmed by a runaway relief study before the recipe or the initiator is changed.
        • Any change — a new initiator, a faster recipe, a bigger charge, a new cleaning method — goes through management of change, which checks whether the HAZOP must be updated.
        • Revalidate the HAZOP periodically (typically every five years) and after incidents or near misses.
        • Use the simulator to train operators on the scenarios this HAZOP found and to check that the alarm responses and procedures work in time.

        Safety layers · layers of protection for R-101

        Teaching slide deck · Safety layers — the six layers on the R-101 P&ID, the short-stop SIS and its cause-and-effect matrix, the operating window, independence and relief of a runaway reactor.
        Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

        Safety must cover failures of equipment (including control) and of people, and more than one failure at a time. The response should be limited, keeping production where possible. So protection is built in layers, each independent of the others, with more strength held in reserve as the event gets more serious. Source: course 2105625 Process Safety (safety hierarchy), applied to the batch PVC reactor R-101. Settings come from the model (K) and the page's alarm table; values marked "assumed" are for teaching.

        1 The six layers · 2 P&ID layer by layer · 3 What each layer does · SIS cause-and-effect · 4 Integrity operating window · 5 Independence check · 6 Good practices · 7 Standards

        1 · The six layers

        LayerJob on R-101Automatic?Needs power / computer?Needs a person?
        1 BPCSHolds 57 °C against the heat release (cascade, split range, VPC-130), runs the batch sequenceYesYesSupervises
        2 AlarmsBring a drifting temperature, pressure, level or circulation to a personNo actionYesYes: decides
        3 SISKill the reaction with the short-stop, close the charges, full coolingYesYes (de-energise to trip — but XV-104 needs air to open)No (reset only)
        4 ReliefPSV-100 to D-103 before the vessel failsYes, self-actuatingNoNo
        5 ContainmentKeep VCM in closed recovery; detect and isolate a leakPassive or remoteMostly noPartly
        6 Emergency responseDeluge, water curtain, evacuation, first aidNoPartlyYes

        Layers 1–4 are the independent protection layers of the automation. Layers 1–3 need electrical power, computing and communication, so one power or computer failure could take out all three at once; that is why SIS valves go to their fail position without power and relief, containment and emergency response are kept in reserve. On R-101 the chemical "kill" of the SIS acts by opening a valve, so instrument air joins power as a common cause (section 5). Click a ring to open that layer on the P&ID.

        R-101 redrawn in the coordinates of the simulator P&ID.         SIS cause-and-effect matrix (layer 3), live

        Effects read from bmsTrip(), bmsStep() and step() in the model. "ACTIVE" = the condition of tripConditions(sim) is true now; "FIRST-OUT" = the cause latched in sim.P.sis.first (after a trip the conditions often clear because the reaction has been stopped, so the first-out is what stays).

        4 · Integrity operating window

        Each key variable has a target, alarm limits that still leave time to act, an SIS limit, relief and a critical limit where failure comes quickly. Temperature and pressure are tied together by the VCM vapour pressure while free monomer exists, so the pressure settings appear on the temperature ladder as the temperatures at which they are reached (computed from the model's vapour pressures with the design-state inerts). The arrow is the live value: load a training exercise and watch it climb through the layers. Critical limits not in the design data are marked "assumed".

        5 · Independence check

        A layer must not share its sensor, logic or final element with the layer below, or one failure defeats both. The SIS column says which measurement tripConditions() actually reads — the drawing alone can mislead. An alarm that is the pre-alarm of a trip may share the trip's sensor, but LOPA then credits only one of them.

        7 · Standards

        • IEC 61511 / ISA-84: SIS life cycle, safety requirements specification (the C&E above), independence, SIL, proof testing. CCPS Layer of Protection Analysis and Guidelines for Safe Automation of Chemical Processes.
        • ISA-18.2 / EEMUA 191: alarm philosophy, priorities, rationalisation, suppression by operating state, alarm rates.
        • API 520 / API 521 and ASME VIII Div. 1: relief sizing and installation, set pressure ≤ MAWP, 110 % accumulation, inlet and back-pressure limits, rupture discs.
        • DIERS (AIChE Design Institute for Emergency Relief Systems) and CCPS Guidelines for Pressure Relief and Effluent Handling Systems: two-phase relief of a runaway reactor, vent sizing, catch tank D-103.
        • CCPS Guidelines for Process Safety in Batch Reaction Systems and Essential Practices for Managing Chemical Reactivity Hazards: short-stop, emergency cooling and agitation of batch polymerisation.
        • NFPA 15 (water spray and deluge), NFPA 72 (fire and gas alarm), NFPA 30 / NFPA 58 guidance on liquefied flammable gas handling; the owner's emergency response plan.
        • Thai Department of Industrial Works: regulation on hazard identification, risk assessment and risk management plans (B.E. 2543) and on the safety of factories handling hazardous chemicals.

        Part A · Reliability for safety

        A1 · Definitions

        TermMeaningOn R-101
        HazardInherent physical or chemical characteristic that can harm people, environment or property (CCPS)51 t of VCM (flammable, carcinogenic, liquefied under pressure) polymerising with 71 kJ/mol of heat
        Hazardous eventRelease of material or energy that can cause harmRunaway to relief or vessel rupture; VCM loss of containment
        RiskRisk = consequence × frequencyA fatality (severity 5) tolerable only below 10−4 /yr (course criteria)
        Tolerable / residual riskRisk accepted in context / risk left after protectionThe LOPA target frequency / the mitigated frequency of the worksheet
        Reliability R(t)Probability of success during an interval of timeThe short-stop SIF still able to act at the end of a one-year proof-test interval
        PFDProbability of failure on demand; F(t) = 1 − R(t)The chance that XV-104 does not inject when TSHH-101 trips
        Deterministic / probabilistic analysisCan the design keep events within limits / what is the numerical risk and is it tolerablePSV-100 sized for the runaway (DIERS) / LOPA below

        Is 99.9 % reliability good enough? R-101 runs about batches a year; a 1-in-1000 failure per batch would be more than one event a year on one reactor. Safety needs both plant reliability (business continuity) and safety reliability (hazard prevention and mitigation).

        A2 · Failure rate from a population

        λ = ΔNf / (Ns · Δt): failures in the interval divided by the survivors and the interval length. 100 identical units (think of 100 short-stop valves) are drawn from a Weibull life model R(t) = e−(t/α)β at the quantiles ti = α(−ln(1 − (i − 0.5)/100))1/β, shuffled with a seeded generator so the picture is stable. β < 1 is burn-in, β = 1 the useful life (constant λ = 1/α, the exponential model), β > 1 wear-out.

        A3 · R(t), PFD and proof testing

        With a constant failure rate R(t) = e−λt and PFD(t) = F(t) = 1 − e−λt ≈ λt when PFD ≪ 0.1. A standby safeguard such as XV-104 fails unseen, so its PFD grows until the next proof test restores it: PFDavg = (1/T)∫0T(1 − e−λt)dt = 1 − (1 − e−λT)/(λT) ≈ λT/2. MTTF = ∫R dt = 1/λ.

        SIL (IEC 61511, demand mode)PFDavgRRF
        SIL 110−2 – 10−110 – 100
        SIL 210−3 – 10−2100 – 1 000
        SIL 310−4 – 10−31 000 – 10 000

        A4 · Reliability block diagrams and the R-101 SIFs

        ConfigurationPFDReliabilityFailure rate / MTTFPFDavg over test interval T
        Series (multi-component): any failure fails the pathPFDA + PFDBR1·R2λ = λ1 + λ2; MTTF = 1/(λ1+λ2)λT/2 (1oo1); λT (2oo2)
        Parallel (redundancy): all paths must failPFDA × PFDBR1+R2−R1R2MTTF = 1/λ1+1/λ2−1/(λ1+λ2)(λT)²/3 (1oo2)
        2-out-of-3 (complex system)PFDAPFDB+PFDBPFDC+PFDCPFDA——(λT)²

        SIF calculator. A safety instrumented function is sensor → logic solver → final element in series; each subsystem can be redundant. On R-101 the final element of the short-stop is not just a valve: XV-104 with its solenoid, the N₂-pressurised pot D-105 and the injection line must all work. Pick an interlock, change the voting, the SIS-grade failure rates (λDU) or the test interval. Improving reliability: diversity (TE-101 and PT-101 see the same runaway by different physics), separation (no single point of failure), fail-safe design (hard here: the short-stop must open a valve).

        SubsystemVotingλDU per channel (/yr)PFDavgShare

        The course method for parallel systems. Three layers against the same hazard, each with an equivalent failure rate (sum of its blocks), combined as parallel systems through MTTF (inclusion–exclusion): 1/λsys = Σ1/λi − Σ1/(λi+λj) + 1/(λ1+λ2+λ3).
