A generic rate counts all failure modes; an SIS rate counts only dangerous undetected failures of certified equipment, so a generic rate must not be put into λT/2 for a SIF. Rows marked "assumed" are PVC-specific teaching values.

        Part B · Layers of protection analysis (LOPA)

        B1 · The method

        1. Take a scenario from the HAZOP (cause → consequence) and rate its severity; the severity sets the target frequency.
        2. Estimate the initiating event frequency (IEF) from failure data. If several causes lead to the same consequence, work each and add the frequencies. A per-batch human error becomes a yearly frequency through the number of batches.
        3. Credit each independent protection layer (IPL) with its PFD. A layer that shares a component with the initiating event, or with another credited layer, gets no credit.
        4. Apply enabling events (time at risk) and conditional modifiers (probability of ignition, occupancy, probability of fatality).
        5. Compare with the target: RRF = f / target. If RRF > 1 the gap sets the PFD, and so the SIL, of the extra layer.

        Lecture example: pressure control malfunction 0.1 /yr × high-pressure alarm 0.1 × relief valve 0.01 × occupancy 0.1 = /yr against a fatality target of 10−6 /yr → RRF = , not acceptable.

        B2 · Criteria used here (course risk matrix)

        SeverityTarget risk frequency (/yr)Health and safetyEnvironmentEconomic

        Likelihood levels by frequency: 5 most likely (~10 /yr), 4 likely (~1), 3 possible (~0.1), 2 rare (~0.01), 1 almost impossible (~0.001); the band boundaries are taken halfway between decades (on a log scale). Risk = severity × likelihood: 1 negligible, 2–6 low, 8–12 medium, 15–20 high, 25 extreme. Target frequencies differ by country (for a fatality about 10−4 to 10−6 /yr). This matrix is stricter than the HAZOP tab's S × L banding, which was used only to rank rows.

        B3 · What counts as an IPL

        An IPL must be independent of the initiating event and of the other credited layers, specific to the scenario, dependable (its PFD can be justified — including the time to act: an alarm needs ≥ 10 min between alarm and harm) and auditable (tested). Procedures, training and inspection are safeguards but usually not IPLs. On R-101 one final element (XV-104 with pot D-105) earns one credit, however many trips drive it.

          Part C · Bow-tie

          A bow-tie is several LOPAs drawn around one top event (the moment control of the hazard is lost). Threats on the left pass prevention barriers; consequences on the right sit behind mitigation (recovery) barriers and conditional modifiers. Escalation factors are conditions that defeat a barrier (a bypass, an empty pot, lost air). The top-event frequency is the sum of the threat frequencies times their barrier PFDs. Barrier colours follow the Safety layers tab; grey is design, a procedure or a conditional modifier. Click a barrier to fail it. The barrier values are the worksheet's credits; the bow-tie does not apply the LOPA independence rules, so read it as a picture of the layers, and the worksheet as the number.

          2 · SIF list

          Process safety time (PST): time from the trip point being crossed to the hazardous event (PSV-100 set reached), with no SIF action. Response time: sensor 0.5 s + logic 0.25 s + trip delay + valve stroke 2 s (assumed, TBC). Good practice: response ≤ ½ PST. "Not from model": the lumped, well-mixed reactor does not reach the hazard for that demand, so the time budget rests on the HAZOP. PFDavg is computed live with the LOPA tab's failure data and T = 1 yr and judged against the PFD the LOPA scenario needs from this SIF.

            1 · What a cause and effect diagram is

            • A cause is one sensed condition with its direction and setting (low, high, high-high, stopped, push-button). Alarm-only causes light the amber alarm and sound the horn; trip causes act on the final elements and raise the red SIS alarm.
            • An effect is one action on one device or latch, written as a code in the header row (O open, C close, FO forced open, TP tripped, F first-out, A activate, P permissive). A mark shows which causes drive it.
            • The matrix follows the SRS of each SIF (the SRS of SIF tab), the alarm list and the batch permissives, and must match the logic exactly. Here the effects are read from the simulator's trip functions, and section 5 tests them on copies of the model.

                Transition operation · the batch cycle, grade changes, load following, regeneration and emergencies on R-101

                Teaching slide deck · Transition operation — a batch is a chain of transitions: R-101 from an empty reactor full of air to a discharged batch, step by step with the reasons, then grade changes, load following with four reactors, cleaning and emergency short-stop, all run on the model.
                Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

                Follows the course lecture Operating during Transition (Process Operation). A transition is the planned transient between an initial and a final condition. A continuous unit spends most of its life at a steady state; a batch reactor never does — every batch is a sequence of transitions, and the reaction step is itself a transient. Every trend and number below comes from scripted runs of this simulator's model (copies, precomputed by tabs/trans/tools/trcomp.js); the live plant is not touched. The graded procedures stay on the Exercises tab.

                1 Transitions · 2 Before a batch · 3 The batch cycle · 3a Evacuation · 3b Heat-up and initiation · 3c End point and short-stop · 3d Degassing · 4 Grade change · 5 Load following · 6 Regeneration and storage · 7 Emergency transitions · 8 What makes it hard

                1 · What a transition is, and which ones R-101 has

                Transitions are planned transient behaviour between different initial and final conditions. They need their own procedures, sequence logic, permissives and sometimes extra equipment, because the equipment is sized for the reaction and the plant is protected for the reaction. For a batch reactor the list is longer than for a continuous unit: the batch itself is the first transition.

                  3 · The batch cycle: the order and the reasons

                  The script below does what the graded cold-start and end-of-batch procedures ask (the same steps as src/expert.js): start from an empty, washed reactor full of air with every controller in manual, run the batch sequence through the SIS commands, and finish with an empty reactor. The durations are the model's.

                  No.StepWhy this order (analysis)Safety concernModel

                  3a · Evacuation: why the air must come out first, and how far

                  Oxygen left in the reactor does two things: it inhibits the polymerisation (radicals react with O₂ before they react with VCM, so the batch shows an induction period) and it forms polymeric peroxides with VCM, unstable compounds that can decompose violently in vents, recovery lines and the gasholder. The inerts (N₂ from the air) also stay in the vapour space: they add their partial pressure to the VCM vapour pressure and collect in E-101. The same script was run with the vacuum pump stopped at different pressures:

                  3b · Heat-up on steam, and when the initiator goes in

                  After the charge the batch sits at the mixing temperature of hot water and cold VCM. LP steam injected into the jacket loop (TV-110A, the lower half of the TIC-110 split range) heats it; the initiator permissive asks for TI-100 ≥ 54 °C and the procedure initiates at 56.8 °C with the jacket inlet below 62 °C, so the reaction clock starts at the grade temperature and the jacket is ready to cool. Seven heat-up and initiation strategies:

                  3c · End point and short-stop: when to stop the batch

                  While free liquid VCM exists (X < Xf = ) the pressure is the VCM vapour pressure at the batch temperature. Past Xf the monomer is only dissolved in swollen polymer and the pressure falls: the pressure drop is the conversion measurement. PD-100 marks the end point when PI-100 has fallen bar below its running maximum. Stopping earlier wastes VCM (more to recover); stopping later buys conversion slowly, lowers the grain porosity (the pores fill with polymer made in a monomer-starved gel) and costs cycle time. Short-stop moments compared on the same batch:

                  3d · Degassing: the unreacted VCM goes to recovery before the slurry leaves

                  After the short-stop XV-105 opens and HIC-105 throttles the flow to the VCM recovery header. The discharge valve XV-106 is interlocked shut until PI-100 is below 2 bar g, because VCM dissolved at pressure would flash in the blowdown tank D-102. The rate is set by the valve opening and by the pressure the recovery system holds (design bar a): the flow depends on the pressure difference, so the last bar is always the slowest.

                  4 · Blocked operation: grade (K-value) changes

                  The K-value (a measure of chain length) is set almost only by the polymerisation temperature; the model uses K = 67 − 0.62 · (T − 57), averaged over the polymer made. A plant making several grades runs them in blocks (campaigns). For a batch reactor the natural moment to change is between batches: the next batch simply gets a new temperature and recipe, and no transition material is made. Changing the set point within a batch makes a blend. Both were run:

                  What changes with the gradeOn R-101

                  5 · Load following: reactors in service × cycle time

                  A continuous unit follows the load by changing its feed rate. A batch reactor cannot run "at 80 %": each batch is the same 43 t. The train follows demand with the number of reactors in service and the cycle time (a slower or faster recipe), and the downstream stripper and dryer, which are continuous, are fed from the slurry tank. Production = N × PVC per batch × operating hours ÷ cycle time.

                  Staggering the four reactors

                  Four reactors started at the same time would ask for four heat-release peaks together from the same cooling-water system and would all degas into the same recovery header together. Staggered by a quarter of the cycle, the demands overlap less. The curve adds four copies of the scripted batch's heat removal, shifted by the offset:

                  6 · Regeneration: wall build-up, coating and cleaning; storage

                  Polymer deposits on the reactor wall, baffles and E-101 tubes lower heat transfer. In a heat-removal-limited reactor they cost production, because the fastest safe recipe is set by the cooling. The lecture's strategies: parallel equipment (four reactors — one is cleaned while three run), storage (D-102 feeds the stripper while reactors are out), or shutdown.

                  Regeneration or maintenanceWhyWhat is doneHazards and how they are handledStrategy

                  Wall build-up in the model

                  How often to clean? (build-up per batch and cleaning time are assumed)

                  Slurry tank D-102: how much hold-up?

                  The stripper downstream runs continuously; D-102 turns the batch discharges into a steady feed and covers a stripper outage while the reactors keep discharging. Hold-up V = F · t, plus one batch that can arrive at any moment.

                  7 · Emergency transitions: short-stop, emergency vent, loss of agitation

                  The one transition that is never planned in time, only in method. A reacting batch holds its energy as unreacted monomer: t of VCM at the design state (2.0 h into the reaction) still hold . The emergency transitions therefore stop the source (short-stop kills the radicals), maximise the sink (all cooling forced open) and, when pressure must come down, remove the inventory (emergency vent). The actions are those of the model's bmsTrip() and step():

                    Process reliability · how many batches R-101 loses, and how to lose fewer

                    Teaching slide deck — reliability, failure rate and availability, series / parallel / standby / k-of-N structures, R-101 as a series system for production, design and maintenance for reliability, inventory and life-cycle cost, all on the R-101 model.
                    Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

                    Follows the course material on reliability (T. Marlin, Operability in Process Design, Ch. 4 Reliability; the Introduction to Reliability Engineering course: failure statistics, MTTF/MTBF, series/parallel/k-of-N, critical items). This tab is about the reliability of production: a lost batch costs money and reactor time. The reliability of safeguards (probability of failure on demand of TSHH-101, PSHH-101, the short-stop and PSV-100) is on the LOPA tab. Failure rates are the course's generic all-modes values or assumed values; every fraction, repair time, price and cost marked assumed is a teaching value. Numbers marked model come from runs of this simulator (copies of the design state, never the live batch).

                    1 Definitions · 2 Failure rate and life · 3 Structures and the standby warning · 4 R-101 as a series system · 5 Design for reliability · 6 Wall build-up and the wash interval · 7 Inventory: D-102 · 8 Maintenance · 9 Life-cycle cost of jacket pumps · 10 Reactor reliability audit

                    1 · Reliability, availability and why they differ

                    Availability is not reliability. A reactor that loses twelve batches a year but is washed and recharged within a shift can still show 98 % availability; every lost batch is still 43 t of PVC not made, a short-stopped batch to degas and sell off-grade, and a wash. Reliability counts the events, availability counts the time.

                    2 · Failure rate, the bathtub and the exponential model

                    Failure rate λ(t) = failures per unit time ÷ items still working. Over a life it often follows the bathtub: infant mortality (falling λ), chance failures (constant λ), wear-out (rising λ). Most equipment does not show the full bathtub (the RCM studies found six patterns, most without wear-out), so the right maintenance depends on the pattern. With constant λ:

                    R(t) = e−λt,  F(t) = 1 − R(t),  MTTF = 1/λ

                    At t = MTTF only 36.8 % survive. For R-101: P-101A at λ = 2 /yr (course generic) has MTTF = 0.5 yr ≈ 4380 h ≈ 635 batch cycles; the chance it runs through one 6.9 h cycle is e−2×6.9/8000 = 99.83 %.

                    Weibull: R(t) = exp[−(t/η)β], λ(t) = (β/η)(t/η)β−1. Move β through 1 to see the three regions of the bathtub.

                    3 · Structures: series, parallel, standby, k out of N

                    A plant is many components joined in structures; the structure sets the system reliability. The formulas assume independent failures (no common cause) and, for standby, a perfect switch.

                    The standby warning: P-101B is a spare, not a hot standby

                    The chapter's warning fits R-101 exactly. The jacket loop has two pumps; P-101A runs and P-101B is started by the operator. While the batch reacts, FSLL-110 short-stops it when FI-110 stays below m³/h for s. A suspension batch at 57 °C cannot ride through a loss of jacket circulation for long, so the spare only saves the batch if it is running inside the window. The model runs below stop P-101A on the design state (2 h into the reaction) and start P-101B Δ seconds later (pvBatch from the design state, 30 min, SIS on).

                    A person as the switch. Detecting the FI-110 alarm, recognising the cause and starting P-101B is a human response with a spread. Take the operator's response time as lognormal (assumed; set its median and spread):

                    4 · R-101 as a series system: what loses a batch, and how often

                    For production every element in the chain must work through the batch: agitation, jacket circulation, cooling water, instrument air, power, initiator, the charge and vacuum equipment, VCM recovery, and no spurious trip of TSHH-101, PSHH-101, FSLL-110 or XS-101. R-101 is a series system: λsys = Σ λi fi, where fi is the fraction of element i's failures (all modes) that loses a batch. Consequence of each lost batch (assumed): the reactor time already spent (on average half-way through the reaction, h), a wash and inspection ( h), plus the repair time when R-101 cannot restart without the item. Tick the design changes:

                    5 · Design for reliability

                    "There is no safe side in equipment sizing." An oversized jacket pump runs left of its best-efficiency point: recirculation, vibration, seal and bearing failures. An oversized agitator drive runs at low load but its seal still sees full pressure. Match the equipment to its service; spare the items that fail often and that the batch cannot ride through.

                    6 · Operating for reliability: wall build-up and the wash interval

                    PVC deposits on the reactor wall insulate it from the jacket; in the model a full build-up (wall_foul) lowers the jacket U by 45 %. At the design initiator dose the batch time hardly changes, because the other heat sinks still have room. The build-up therefore does not show up as lost time: it costs cooling margin at the peak of the batch, and margin is what lets a plant use a faster recipe. The lab runs every batch at the highest dose that keeps the peak jacket CW valve opening (TV-110B) at or below the limit you set — the design-sweep measure of margin (65 pvBatch runs from the start of the reaction, SIS off: dose 0.8–1.4 × design × build-up 0, 25, 50, 75, 100 %), lets the build-up grow linearly with the batches since the last wash (assumed) and washes the reactor every N batches.

                    Assumed: linear build-up, the non-reaction part of the cycle 1.63 h (design basis 6.9 h − 5.27 h), dose capped at 1.4 × design (the grid). The model has no porosity or K-value penalty for a faster recipe at the same temperature; a real plant checks grain quality before moving the dose.

                    7 · Reliability through inventory: D-102 between the reactors and the stripper

                    The four reactors discharge batches of slurry into the blowdown tank D-102; the stripper and dryer take it out continuously. A tank between an unreliable unit and the next one lets the next unit run while the first is repaired. With the upstream repair time exponential (mean MTTR) and a holdup τ = V/F, the chance that one outage is covered is 1 − e−τ/MTTR, so Rsys = R₂[R₁ + (1 − R₁)(1 − e−τ/MTTR)]. The feed to the stripper follows from the model batch: .

                    The same tank works the other way: when the stripper stops, D-102 must have free volume for the next discharges, or the reactors hold finished batches and the cycle stretches. A tank kept half full buffers both directions. Inventory has a price: capital, a larger hazardous inventory (residual VCM in slurry), and slurry that settles if it is not agitated.

                    8 · Maintenance for reliability

                    9 · Life-cycle cost: how many jacket pumps per reactor?

                    Life-cycle costing adds the costs that reliability changes: capital and maintenance of the extra equipment, failure frequency and the cost of each failure. For R-101 a pump failure costs a lost batch (value from part 4) and, with no spare, the repair time too. Prices, pump cost and the auto-start kit are assumed teaching values.

                    The checks a reactor team makes before failures occur, with this model's numbers (all model runs: pvCapacity holds every cooling handle wide open for 300 s from the state named; ride-through runs use pvBatch with the SIS on unless stated).

Barringer, Life Cycle Cost Tutorial (1996); CCPS, Guidelines for Process Equipment Reliability Data (1989); NASA, Reliability Centered Maintenance Guide (2000); B.S. Dhillon, Reliability, Quality and Safety for Engineers (2005).

                    1 Efficiency and priorities · 2 The batch now and the reference batch · 3 Initiator dose and the heat-removal limit · 4 Cooling water and wall build-up · 5 End-point choice · 6 Energy and monomer options · 7 Pushing toward the constraint · 8 Key energy variables (live)

                    1 · Efficiency, optimisation and their place among the priorities

                    Efficiency (in operation the same as optimisation) is good economic performance: more on-grade product per reactor-hour, less monomer lost, less energy, less effluent. For energy, efficiency = useful output ÷ total input, and a chain of steps multiplies: the lecture's boiler 90 % × turbo-generator 40 % × transmission 90 % = 32.4 %.

                    Four ways to get it (lecture): design with the right capacities; use the equipment in the most efficient way; choose better structures (recover monomer and heat); choose the best operating conditions inside the window. For a batch reactor the scarce resource is usually the reactor-hour: part 2 shows energy is a few per cent of the margin, while a shorter cycle is worth as much as a bigger reactor.

                    Efficiencies multiply along the chain

                    3 · Initiator dose: batch time against the heat-removal limit

                    The initiator dose sets the radical flux, so it sets how fast the batch runs. Classical kinetics (rp ∝ √[I]) gives the rule of thumb t ∝ dose−½. A faster batch releases the same 49 GJ in less time, so the peak heat release rises and the cooling must follow: the reflux condenser takes most of the rise, but the jacket CW valve TV-110B has to cover what the condenser has not yet picked up, and once it reaches 100 % the temperature can no longer be held. The sweep: dose 0.6–1.5 × design, 19 batch runs per condition.

                    4 · Cooling-water temperature and wall build-up move the limit

                    At the design dose neither a warmer CW supply nor a fouled wall changes the batch time much: the temperature controllers hold 57 °C and the heat goes elsewhere. What they change is the margin, and so the highest dose (and shortest batch) the cooling allows. The bars below take, for each condition, the highest dose within the limits set in part 3.

                    5 · Where to stop: the end-point choice

                    The end point is PD-100: PI-100 falls a set amount below its running maximum after the free monomer phase disappears (X ≈ 0.72). A small drop stops early (less PVC, more VCM to recover, shorter cycle); a large one runs on into the slow tail of the gel phase. Runs with the end-point setting at 1.0, 1.4, 1.8 (design), 2.2 and 2.5 bar:

                    6 · Energy and monomer options, sized for R-101

                    Per reactor and for the train of four at the prices of part 2 (training prices) and 8000 h/yr. Where the model can give the number it does; otherwise the basis is stated.

                    Hot-water charge against a cold charge (model heat-up runs)

                    Jacket pump P-101: throttling against speed control (illustration)

                    7 · Best operating conditions: push toward the constraint, but only as far as the variability allows

                    Many conditions do not affect safety or quality but do affect profit; the best value usually sits against a constraint, and how close you can go depends on variability (the lecture's cracking furnace; the fired heater's O₂ set point against CO). Here the constraint is heat removal at the peak and the variability is the initiator activity from lot to lot: a batch charged at dose dset with a lot of activity a = 1 + ε (ε normal, σ) behaves like dose dset·a. It is over the limit when dset·a > dlim: P = ½ erfc[(dlim/dset − 1)/(σ√2)]. dlim comes from part 3 (condition and limits set there).

                    Industrial practice: reduce the variability first (lot testing, dosing accuracy, a stable CW supply), then move the set point; move it slowly and check product quality (grain porosity, K-value) at each step; keep a way out (the short-stop) when a batch goes over.

                    8 · Energy monitoring: key energy variables of R-101 (live)

                    A plant energy dashboard tracks the specific consumption (energy per tonne of product) against a benchmark and the key energy variables (KEV) that move it. Benchmarks are the reference batch (model); the page's alarm limits come from ALM.

                    References: course lecture Process Efficiency (Process Operation); T. Marlin, Process Operability class materials; US DOE, Improving Pumping System Performance (affinity laws, VSD); textbook kinetics of free-radical suspension polymerisation (rate ∝ √[I], gel effect).

                    1 What an SOP is · 2 Format · 3 SOP register · 4 SOP viewer · 5 Writing rules · 6 Life of an SOP

                    1 · What an SOP is, and which activities need one

                    A standard operating procedure is the written, approved way to carry out one task: the same steps, in the same order, with the same checks, whoever is on shift. It turns the reasons worked out on the other tabs — the batch order, the permissives, the operating window, the trips — into actions an operator can follow at 3 a.m. under pressure.

                    A batch reactor needs more SOPs than a continuous unit of the same size: every batch runs the whole start-up and shut-down — about forty operator actions — and the reactor holds a flammable, toxic monomer with a large stored heat of reaction. The US process safety management standard lists what must be written down; the Thai Ministry of Industry notification on process safety management (B.E. 2543) asks for written operating procedures in the same way.

                    6 · The life of an SOP

                    Draft from the design intent and the hazard studies (HAZOP, LOPA) → verify on the simulator (the graded procedures run the same steps against the model) → review by operations, process and safety → approve and train → use, with deviations reported → review after any change (management of change: a new grade, a new trip setting, a new initiator), after an incident, or at a fixed interval (typically 1–3 years; OSHA asks for annual certification that procedures are current).

                    1 · Purpose and outcomes

                    After these sessions you should be able to run a PVC suspension batch from an empty reactor to discharge, hold the reaction temperature within ± 0.5 °C, read the heat balance and the cooling margin, recognise the end point from the pressure, handle the common upsets (lost agitation, lost cooling, inerts, fouling, instrument faults) and decide when a batch must be short-stopped.

                    4 · Safety systems and alarms

                    5 · Operating rules

                    • Never charge VCM into a reactor that has not been evacuated; never open the bottom valve above 2 bar g.
                    • Charge the initiator only with the reactor at 54–57 °C and the jacket inlet below about 75 °C (overshoot).
                    • Bring E-101 in gradually after the reaction starts; vent its inerts when it comes into service and whenever TI-132 falls well below the reactor temperature.
                    • Watch the margin: TV-110B above 90 % with E-101 near its maximum means the next disturbance cannot be absorbed.
                    • If the temperature keeps rising with every cooler at maximum, short-stop — do not wait for the SIS at 63 °C.
                    • Never run the batch without agitation. If the agitator stops, the batch is short-stopped; restart it only to mix the short-stop.
                    • Short-stop at the end point (PD-100 1.8 bar); do not degas a batch that is still reacting.

                    6 · Activities

                    Part A · Familiarisation. Complete the DCS reading sheet (Exercises tab). Sketch the heat balance at design from the Heat removal display and check it against section 7 of the Process tab.

                    Part B · What-if and trends. Do three what-if events and the trend matching; explain each direction with the heat balance.

                    Part C · Cold start (procedure):

                      Part D · End of batch (procedure):

                        Part E · Training exercises. For each exercise note the first alarm, what moved, the cause and your action.

                        Part F · Think EQUIPPED troubleshooting. For each case write the six stages: Engage (what is at stake), Define (the real problem, in numbers), Explore (hypotheses and the checks that separate them), Plan, Do it, Look back.

                        Part G · Data and report. Export the run data of one graded procedure and plot TI-101, PI-100, XI-100 and the three duties against time.

                        • One troubleshooting case written in six stages.
                        • What you would change in the procedure or the control scheme.

                        5 · Differences between the sheets, the drawing above and the simulator

                        • SIS action A: the sheet table says "close XV-101/102/103". The simulator closes XV-101, XV-102 and the vacuum valve XV-109; XV-103 (initiator) is only open during the 60 s dose, so it is already shut.
                        • LSHH-100 is drawn on the LT-100 radar loop on sheet 001; the simulator trips on its own level measurement, independent of LIC-100's transmitter (the Safety layers tab's independence check uses the simulator's behaviour).
                        • Instrument-air failure: the sheets draw XV-104 and XV-108 as fail-closed on/off valves, so they cannot open without air. In the simulator the short-stop still reaches the reactor after an air failure, as if a dedicated air receiver were fitted (HAZOP recommendation; see the HAZOP and Safety layers tabs).

                        Batch sequence and safety instrumented system · R-101

                        EMPTY

                        Commands open the sequence valves once their permissives are met; the totalisers close XV-101/102 at the presets. The short-stop can be injected by the operator at any time and is injected by the SIS on a trip. After a trip: keep the agitator and full cooling, clear the cause, reset, then degas and discharge — a short-stopped batch cannot be restarted.

                            Procedure tracker

                            What-if exercise

                            Predict the direction each variable moves 30 minutes after the event, starting from the design batch with all controllers in normal mode. The check compares with an undisturbed copy of the same batch (a batch never stands still).

                            Trend matching

                            Four 10-minute trends from design (event at 0:30). Pens: TI-101 white (54–64 °C), PI-100 green (6–13 bar g), TIC-110 yellow (20–100 °C), FIC-130 magenta (0–600 m³/h), JI-100 cyan (0–450 kW), TI-132 red (20–80 °C).

                            DCS reading sheet

                            Read the current value and the low and high alarm limits for each tag (leave a limit blank if there is none), then check.

                            Download run data as CSV

                            Every simulated second of this session is recorded (up to 8 hours). Times are simulated time from the start of the session.
